accept.prose:
The clerk took the slip back across the counter, turned it to read the seal, and pulled the ledger toward her.

"Mossback Warrens, level one. Solo, is it?" She was already writing his name in. "You cleared two contracts today and took a knock doing it, by the look of that leg. I log what you take, mind, not what I'd take." The pen finished, she stamped the slip and handed it back over — the Guild seal fresh in green wax, the paper still warm from the press. "Payout's on the slip. Seal shows ready when the level's cleared, and you bring it back here. No trophies wanted."

She tucked the ledger away and glanced at the window, where the light was going blue behind the shutters.

"First light's sensible. The warrens are an hour's walk east if the track's not churned, and goblins see in the dark better than you do." Then, to the other question: "Bed? Marla's got rooms over the inn side, two silver the night with supper, and she'll feed you whether you've sense or not. Ask at the kitchen door, not the taproom — the taproom'll lie to you." A beat, and the dry smile again. "Tell her Dace sent you at closing time and she'll know where you've been standing all evening."

Behind him the wet adventurer from the door was arguing about eel-hound prices now, and the rain kept working at the shutters. Through the archway to the inn side, the kitchen smell was stronger — bread and onions and something with bones in it — and lamplight spilled down a short passage toward it.

manual.prose:
Downstairs, the common room was in its evening swell — carters again, a pair of drovers, the smell of the fire and wet wool. Alaric took bread and cheese standing at the kitchen door, and set out while the light still held.

The road to Ashbridge ran through hedged farmland, then along a stream with willows dragging in the current. He passed a haywain, a boy driving geese, a shrine-post with a worn carving nobody had repainted in years. The walls of Ashbridge came up out of the dusk with torches already lit along the gate, and the gate guard waved him through with the disinterest of a man who had counted a hundred travelers that day.

The Guild hall was quieter than the evening before. A lamplighter was working the brackets outside; inside, Dace was at her counter with the spectacles pushed up into her grey hair, and the pelt-haggler had gone, leaving the floor waxed and empty around the board.

Alaric laid his question at the counter. Dace looked at him a moment.

"Primer of Mend. We keep a shelf." She fetched a slim book from beneath the counter — plain cover, stitched spine, the first page a block of careful script and a diagram of joined hands. "One-twenty copper. It's the basic joining-cantrip, the one every caravan master wishes his people had. Reading won't do it for you in an afternoon, mind — you'll get what you work for."

She took the coins, counted them, and stamped the inside cover with the Guild's minor-issue mark. "Ours on loan no — bought is bought. Bring it back when you've no use for it and I'll give you forty for it."

Alaric took it to a bench by the window, where the last of the lamplight fell on the page. The opening chapters were patience itself: breath, the shape of the power in the mind, the small closed feeling of it drawn to the fingertips. He worked through the first exercises until the hall emptied around him and Dace began stacking stools, the words still plain on the page, the power still just out of his fingers' reach.

payout.prose:
The walk down out of the pine slope was slower than the walk up. His armor hung heavy on shoulders that had taken the chief's blows, and every hedgerow crossing and stile reminded his ribs of it. A carter going the same way with an empty wagon looked at him once — the blood, the crude sword hanging from his fist — and flicked his reins up a little without a word.

Ashbridge took him in at the east gate with the usual nod to the guard, and the streets were at their midday noise: bakers' smoke, a dog trotting off with a bone, two boys hauling water and arguing about who'd spill it. The Guild hall stood where it always stood, its door propped open to the smell of parchment and wet cloaks.

The hall was half-full. A grey-bearded carter was backing a loaded cart toward the trade door, and near the front desk a merchant in a good coat was leaning over a pelt, saying, "That's winter hide, that is, look at the density — you're not getting winter price for autumn wear," while the clerk behind the counter, heavyset and patient, waited him out with his eyes elsewhere.

His eyes found Alaric as he came up. "Back again. You look like the hill argued." He took the two slips when Alaric laid them on the counter, ran his thumb over each seal, and grunted. "Both Mossback. Level one cleared." He turned to the ledger, made two marks, and counted out coin — first the smaller stack, then the larger, pushing both across the wood together. "Sixty and a hundred twenty copper. That's the warrens square. The seal takes a day to fade to done, so mind nobody offers you the same hill twice."

The merchant glanced over at the words, took in the crude goblin blade, and went back to his pelts.
